title: In 1994 a tree new to science turned up in a gorge just 150 km from Sydney
body: In September 1994, David Noble and two companions exploring canyons in Wollemi National Park came across trees nobody had ever described. Despite its name, the **Wollemi pine** is not a pine at all: it belongs to the Araucariaceae, and is one of only three living genera in that family. It is often called a 'living fossil', though no fossil can be pinned on it for certain. The wild grove is so precious that its location is still kept from the public.

cover.alt: A tall Wollemi pine against a blue sky, its fern-like branches tipped with round green cones

slides.prompt: How many adult Wollemi pines are known to grow in the wild?
slides.detail: They grow in four locations not far apart. Counting is tricky, because most trees have several trunks that may share one root system.

slides.heading: Copies of copies
slides.text: Every wild tree tested so far is genetically indistinguishable from the others. That suggests the species squeezed through a bottleneck between about 10,000 and 26,000 years ago, possibly down to just one or two individuals.

slides.heading: Saving a tree that hid for ages

events.text: Found in sandstone gorges in Wollemi National Park
The root-rot mould *Phytophthora* is found in wild trees
Young trees go to Australian botanic gardens
Firefighters save the grove from bushfires

slides.heading: How tall Wollemi pines grow
slides.note: Wild trees reach 25 to 40 m; the garden record, in France, was 8.1 m at 14 years old

slides.question: Why are wild Wollemi pines almost genetically identical?
options: The species went through a bottleneck
They were planted from one seed
They are hybrids of two species
slides.explanation: Thousands of years ago the population probably crashed to a tiny number of trees, so all of today's trees descend from very few ancestors.
